Self-introduction

Who I am as an engineer

Part 1 of my Engineers in Society e-portfolio. Written for future employers as much as for assessment.

In short: I'm a petroleum engineer who wants to work where oil and gas actually leaves the reservoir: production operations, ideally in the field. This portfolio records how I got here and reflects honestly on what I've achieved against my programme outcomes, where I still fall short, and how I plan to keep learning.

Shaped by many places

My education has moved across three countries. I sat my IGCSEs at GEMS Westminster School in Sharjah, began A Levels at Cambridge International School in Dubai, finished them at Future World School in Islamabad, and then came to Kuala Lumpur for my degree at Asia Pacific University, one of the most internationally mixed campuses in the region. I work in English and Urdu and hold conversations in Arabic. Moving that often taught me to adapt quickly, and it taught me that the strongest teams are made of people who see a problem differently. I've learned to treat listening as a technical skill, not a courtesy.

Professionalism I've seen up close

At Descon Engineering's Lahore Manufacturing Works, I rotated through the Proposal, Planning, Design and Production departments while the plant built heat exchangers and pressure vessels for Fatima Fertilizer and ADNOC. There, professionalism was physical. A weld was gouged out and redone because a radiograph showed porosity. A lift could be halted by any rigger who doubted a shackle. On day one I was trained in Behaviour-Based Safety and told that the Stop Authority Rule applied to me, an intern, as much as to anyone. I also worked under strict client-confidentiality and locked-device policies. I left understanding that codes like ASME Section VIII are a promise to the people downstream who will never see the work but trust that it was done properly.

Curious about what's next in energy

I'm drawn to how digital tools are changing production. I was part of Crude Intelligence, a three-person team that won first place in the global AI Hackathon II: GO TECH 2025, and we were invited to present in Dubai. At Descon I saw SAP act as a "digital thread", linking every steel heat number and weld joint to its test record. Across my coursework and field development project I've modelled reservoirs in CMG, tNavigator and Petrel, designed well trajectories in Dobby, and run nodal analysis in Pengtools. My final year research explored a greener route to flow assurance: a biodegradable rhamnolipid biosurfactant combined with silica nanoparticles to improve how waxy crude flows.

Learning independently, thinking critically

That research didn't go the way I expected. The biosurfactant alone cut gel strength by 66.5%, but combining it with nanoparticles made the crude perform worse than untreated oil. I reported that honestly and traced it to poor nanoparticle dispersion, instead of burying it. That result taught me more about experimental design than a clean one would have. Outside the syllabus I've earned IWCF Level 1 and Well Operations Crew Resource Management certification, a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt, and MATLAB and Python training. I keep putting myself in rooms where I can learn: I competed with APU's team at the SPE PetroBowl Asia Pacific Regional Qualifier 2025 at Universiti Teknologi PETRONAS, and most recently attended the Malaysia STEM Leadership Summit in September 2026.

Contributing locally and globally

In Pakistan, I proposed and initiated Energy4me workshops to introduce high-school students to energy and engineering. In Malaysia, I led communications and outreach for the SPE Student Chapter at APU, joined our chapter's beach clean-up, and volunteered at SPE Kuala Lumpur's Sehelai Baju Raya and Industry Charity Iftar programme for children from care homes. Globally, I've worked inside the teams building equipment bound for the UAE and competed against teams from around the world. What I want next is a production or field engineering role where I can learn from experienced crews, keep wells flowing safely and efficiently, and grow into an engineer people trust with their assets. I'm available to start from January 2027.

Eager to learn. Ready to be useful.

Interested in production engineering, well performance and field operations. Open to roles in Malaysia, the Middle East and Pakistan.

Engineering intern, Production and Design

Descon Engineering Limited

Lahore Manufacturing Works, Pakistan. 1 October 2025 to 21 January 2026, 16 weeks. A rotational placement through the full life of heavy static equipment, from the bid to the shipping saddle.

Descon has grown since 1977 from a five-person Lahore office into an EPCC group of more than 22,000 people from over 30 nationalities. LMW, where I was placed, holds ASME U, U2, S and PP stamps and exports boilers, heat exchangers, pressure vessels, columns, skids and platforms to national oil companies such as ADNOC.

Four departments, one project flow

The placement was deliberately rotational, so I saw how each function hands work to the next.

ProposalReading Invitations to Bid and process data sheets; seeing how capacity, certification and cost decide whether LMW bids at all.
PlanningThe control room. Sequencing man-hours and machine time with SAP resource levelling, and the daily 10:00 coordination meeting.
DesignClient specifications for ADNOC and Fatima Fertilizer, P&IDs, shell-and-tube and air-cooled exchanger design, with HTRI, Codeware Compress and Aspen HYSYS in use.
ProductionCNC and radial drilling, rolling, SMAW, SAW and GTAW welding, NDT and hydrotesting on the shop floor.

From bid to shipment

The fabrication sequence I followed at LMW. Keep scrolling to move through it.

1

Invitation to bid

The Proposal team checks the client's process data sheets for temperature, pressure and fluid chemistry, then confirms LMW has the capacity and ASME stamps to deliver before pricing the job.

Engineering starts as a commercial decision
2

Design and client approval

Some ADNOC packages arrive fully designed, so Descon verifies they can be fabricated. For Fatima Fertilizer, Descon designs shell thickness, tube layout and tubesheets itself. Nothing is cut until the client stamps drawings Approved for Construction.

Two parties agree on every safety factor
3

Store and procurement

The bill of materials goes into SAP. Plates such as SA-516 Gr. 70 and SA-213 tubes are checked against stock, and every item must arrive with a Material Test Report proving its chemistry and strength.

Buying steel is a compliance task
4

Layout and cutting

Technicians mark dimensions from approved drawings and cut with CNC oxy-fuel or plasma. A small error in a shell plate's circumference becomes misalignment and a stress point once it's welded.

Precision compounds
5

Rolling and welding

Plates are rolled into shells, braced against ovality, tack welded, then joined with Submerged Arc Welding for deep seams. Thousands of tubes are sealed to tubesheets with GTAW.

Welding treated as a science
6

Pre-heat and stress relief

Plates are pre-heated so the heat-affected zone cools slowly and doesn't form brittle martensite. Finished vessels go into the PWHT furnace at roughly 600 to 650°C to relax residual stress.

A good weld is about grain structure
7

Non-destructive testing

Dye penetrant and magnetic particle tests catch surface cracks between passes. Radiography with Iridium-192 reveals porosity and slag inside critical welds; anything beyond code limits is gouged out and redone.

What you can't see matters most
8

Hydrostatic test

The finished vessel is filled with water and pressurised to 1.3 to 1.5 times its design pressure. Water is incompressible, so a failure here is safe, and it proves the vessel before it ever sees hydrocarbons.

The final gate
9

Data report and shipping

The Manufacturer's Data Report compiles every certificate, weld log and test. Equipment is blasted, given offshore-grade coatings, and moved by route-surveyed heavy-lift convoy from landlocked Lahore to Karachi port.

The data report is the equipment's passport
0bar
The moment it clicked

Watching a vessel prove itself

The most intense thing I witnessed was a hydrostatic test on an ADNOC vessel. Engineers calculated the test pressure from the material's allowable stress at ambient versus operating temperature, then the gauge climbed towards 150 bar.

Seeing the safety factor as a number on a dial, with a room full of people trusting it, did more for my understanding of design margins than any lecture. It's also why I care about operating envelopes: a production engineer is the one who keeps equipment inside them for decades.

In depth

What the placement taught me

Each topic below is something I studied closely at LMW, and why it matters to the production work I want to do.

Heat transfer design and vibrationFatima Fertilizer shell-and-tube exchangers

Fertilizer plants run ammonia and urea synthesis at high temperatures, and the shell-and-tube exchanger is their workhorse. I followed how the design team used HTRI to model convective heat transfer, and how they decide which fluid goes tube-side: usually the corrosive or high-pressure one, because high-alloy small-diameter tubes cost far less than a high-alloy shell.

Baffles support the tubes and create shell-side turbulence, but fast flow can cause flow-induced vibration and tube fatigue. I watched engineers run vibration checks to keep the tubes' natural frequency well above vortex-shedding frequency.

Why it matters in productionExchangers foul, vibrate and leak in service. Knowing how their limits were designed helps me recognise when a change in flow rate is pushing equipment somewhere it shouldn't go.
Sour service metallurgy and sealingADNOC oil and gas vessels

Where hydrogen sulfide is present, carbon steel can suffer hydrogen-induced cracking, so many ADNOC vessels specify HIC-resistant SA-516 Gr. 70 with controlled heat treatment. Others are clad or weld-overlaid inside with stainless steel or Monel, applied by an automated overlay machine, to resist aggressive crude chemistry.

I also learned how much rests on small parts: fully threaded B7 and B16 alloy studs tightened with hydraulic torque wrenches, and gasket seating calculations that compress spiral-wound gaskets enough to seal without crushing them through thermal cycles.

Why it matters in productionH2S, CO2 and corrosion are daily realities on producing fields. Understanding material selection makes me better at integrity management and at asking the right question before changing operating conditions.
ASME Section VIII, Division 1 versus Division 2Design by formula or by analysis

Division 1 uses design-by-formula rules that are conservative and give thicker walls. For ADNOC's high-pressure reactors and separators, the team often used Division 2, which relies on finite element analysis of stresses under combined pressure and thermal loads. That allows a lower design factor and can reduce vessel material weight by up to around 20% at the same level of safety.

Why it matters in productionIt showed me that safety and cost aren't opposites when the analysis is good, a trade-off production engineers face every time they debottleneck a facility.
Welding metallurgy, PWHT and tube jointsHeat-affected zones and residual stress

SAW's heat changes the grain structure of steel next to the weld, leaving a heat-affected zone that can turn brittle in sour service. Induction pre-heating slows cooling and prevents martensite. After welding, I watched a 50-tonne vessel loaded into the PWHT furnace, held at 600 to 650°C and cooled at a controlled rate, which guards against stress corrosion cracking.

Tube-to-tubesheet joints, the most common failure point, were strength-welded with GTAW and then mechanically rolled to close the crevice where corrosion starts. Double-grooved holes add grip in high-vibration service.

Why it matters in productionMany leaks trace back to welds and joints. Knowing how they're made helps me read inspection reports and understand failure causes during troubleshooting.
The digital thread: SAP and traceabilityEvery heat number, every weld, every test

Every plate, tube and stud carries a heat number that is scanned into SAP and linked to its Material Test Report. Each weld joint on a drawing is logged against the welder's certification and electrode batch, and NDT results are recorded against it. The system blocks a project from moving to hydrotesting, or shipping, while a single joint is uncleared.

If equipment fails at a client site years later, that thread traces it back to the mill and the day it was welded.

Why it matters in productionDigital oilfields depend on the same idea: trustworthy data tied to physical assets. This is the kind of emerging technology I want to work with.
The craft of fabricationOvality, alignment and heavy-lift logistics

Thick rolled plate resists a perfect circle. Technicians used spider braces and hydraulic jacks to correct ovality before welding, since an out-of-round shell won't take its head properly. For exchanger bundles, laser levelling kept baffles straight over about 10 metres so tubes could be inserted without scratching.

Getting a finished 30-metre column from Lahore to Karachi takes route surveys of every bridge and power line, coordination with authorities, and modular trailers with many independently steered axles.

Why it matters in productionField work is full of practical constraints that don't appear in calculations. I learned to respect technicians' knowledge as much as engineers'.
Safety as a technical controlBehaviour-Based Safety and the Stop Authority Rule

My placement began with HSE induction and Behaviour-Based Safety training, which focuses on why people take risks: time pressure, overconfidence, habit. The Stop Authority Rule lets anyone halt work, and I saw it treated as a final human sensor. A rigger noticing a frayed wire rope or an uncertified shackle can stop a heavy lift, whatever the deadline.

Why it matters in productionThis is the culture I want to carry to the wellsite. My IWCF Level 1 and crew resource management certifications build on the same principle: speak up early.

Two clients, two engineering philosophies

Fatima Fertilizer

Built for thermal cycles

Plants start up and shut down often, so equipment must survive repeated heating and cooling. The priority is robust tube-to-tubesheet joints, strength-welded and then expanded, and careful thermal design.

ADNOC

Built for pressure and corrosion

Oil and gas service brings high pressure, sour fluids and a salty Gulf atmosphere. The priority is HIC-resistant steel, internal cladding or overlays, rigorous radiography and multi-layer marine coatings.

Critical appraisal

An honest look at the placement

The internship was the most formative part of my degree, but it had limits worth naming.

What worked well

  • The rotation gave me a whole-project view that a single-department internship wouldn't.
  • The HSE culture gave me a safety-first mindset I'll keep.
  • Senior engineers, including the heads of Design and Production, were accessible and willing to explain their decisions.

What held me back

  • Client confidentiality and locked company PCs meant I mostly watched specialist software like HTRI and Codeware Compress in use, rather than running it myself.
  • As an observer on large projects, I had few chances to solve problems independently.
  • The work centred on fabrication, not production operations, so the field side of my ambitions is still ahead of me.

What I recommended to Descon

From my internship report, based on what I saw on the floor and in the design office.

RFID material tracking

Tag plates, tubes and studs in the store so production spends less time searching and traceability in the data report gets even tighter. A practical Industry 4.0 step beyond SAP.

A buddy system for interns

Pair each intern with a junior engineer on one piece of equipment from bid to shipment, instead of seeing fragments of several projects. Include a small intern-owned design task.

Design and inspection cross-talk

Regular sessions between LMW designers and NDT technicians at Inspectest, so designs that tend to produce weld defects are caught earlier.

Final year project

Helping waxy crude flow, more sustainably

Synergistic effects of biosurfactants and nanoparticles on the rheological behaviour and stability of waxy crude oil.

Wax deposition and gelling make waxy crude hard to move through pipelines, and conventional chemical treatments carry environmental costs. I tested a biodegradable rhamnolipid biosurfactant, SiO2 nanoparticles, and both together. Using a Fann 35SA six-speed viscometer at three temperatures, I characterised plastic viscosity, yield point and gel strength with the Bingham plastic model. The research approach was aligned with 12 UN Sustainable Development Goals.

The combined system performed worse than untreated crude. Rather than hide it, I traced the cause to nanoparticle dispersion, a lesson in validating sample preparation that I'll carry into any lab or field test.

Rhamnolipid alone, at 28°C

Gel strength reduction66.5%
Yield point reduction35.3%
Rhamnolipid with SiO2Worse than untreated

Rhamnolipid alone was the only treatment to improve every measured parameter at 28°C.

Teamwork is my lowest outcome

PO9 0.67

How my learning shaped professional conduct

Coursework in HSE and Engineers in Society gave me the vocabulary for professional responsibility, but the internship gave it weight. I saw that legal compliance, such as ASME codes, material traceability and occupational safety law, is not paperwork: it is how a company proves to clients and regulators that people downstream are protected. I also saw inclusive practice working, with Descon's teams drawn from more than 30 nationalities, and APU project groups mixing cultures and learning styles. Taking over communication roles taught me to adapt to visual, verbal and hands-on learners, from high-school students at Energy4me to shop-floor technicians.

How I learn independently

My strongest learning has come from asking why something failed. Descon's radiography rejects, the vibration checks on exchanger tubes, and my own nanoparticle dispersion failure all pushed me to understand mechanisms instead of memorising rules. My weakness is that this learning has been opportunity-driven. The plan below makes it deliberate, and it puts my lowest outcome, teamwork, at the centre.

Areas of excellence

Nine outcomes were fully attained at 1.00: engineering knowledge, investigation, tool usage, society, sustainability, ethics, communication, project management and life-long learning. They're backed by external evidence too: a global hackathon win, an SPE chapter award and industry certifications.

Performance gaps

Individual and team work (PO9, 0.67) is my clearest gap, followed by design (PO3, 0.83) and problem analysis (PO2, 0.90). The first is about how I work with others; the other two are about owning open-ended technical problems rather than observing them.

Reading the scores critically

A 1.00 measures what my assessments asked for, not how I'll perform on a live field. I've treated every full score as a starting line, and noted what it doesn't yet prove.

My continuous development plan

How these reflections turn into action. I'll review progress against it every quarter.

Now to March 2027

Get field-ready

  • Self-study artificial lift, well testing and nodal analysis in depth
  • Build Python production analytics projects on public field data, such as decline curve analysis
  • Complete offshore survival and H2S safety training as target employers require
  • Take a coordinating role in an SPE young professional activity and ask teammates for feedback (PO9)
  • Apply to graduate production and field engineering roles
Years 1 to 2

Learn from the crew

  • Work in a graduate production or field engineering role
  • Learn from operators and technicians first, and take ownership of small design and optimisation tasks (PO3)
  • Register as a graduate engineer with the relevant professional body
  • Stay active in SPE as a young professional
Years 3 to 5

Own the optimisation

  • Lead production optimisation and surveillance work using data-driven tools
  • Contribute to lower-emission operations such as flare and methane reduction
  • Work towards professional engineer status
  • Mentor new graduates and give back through outreach
Part 4

Conclusion

Building this e-portfolio made me look at my degree as evidence rather than a transcript. My PO report card shows full attainment in nine of twelve programme outcomes and an average of 0.95. My strongest growth has been in professionalism: learning that safety authority, honest data, confidentiality and code compliance are responsibilities every engineer carries, whatever their rank.

The scores were also a useful reality check. Teamwork at 0.67 told me something I might otherwise have missed, and design at 0.83 and problem analysis at 0.90 match the gaps I saw myself at Descon and in my research. I've grown as an independent, critical learner, often most from things that didn't work, and I've kept learning beyond the syllabus through IWCF, crew resource management, Lean Six Sigma and emerging technologies like AI and digital traceability.

I'm ready to enter the engineering profession with strong ethical values, an honest view of where I need to improve, and a concrete plan to get there. What I want now is the chance to learn in the field, become a better teammate, and grow into an engineer that crews, clients and communities can trust.
